functions.name: C
functions.summary: Returns the Fresnel cosine integral, the integral of cos(πt²/2) from 0 to x.
description: Numbers can be evaluated with `evaluate`; for a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: S
functions.summary: Returns the Fresnel sine integral, the integral of sin(πt²/2) from 0 to x.
description: Numbers can be evaluated with `evaluate`; for a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: realpart
functions.summary: Returns the real part of a complex expression.
description: Products and sums are multiplied out first. If the real part can't be separated, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: imagpart
functions.summary: Returns the imaginary part of a complex expression.
description: Products and sums are multiplied out first. A real expression gives 0. If the imaginary part can't be separated, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: arg
functions.summary: Returns the argument (angle) of a complex number, from -π to π.
description: It uses [`atan2`](/docs/functions/atan2/), so the quadrant is always right.

functions.name: conjugate
functions.summary: Returns the complex conjugate: i becomes -i.
description: It works through sums, products and powers. In JavaScript it is `nerdamer.conjugate`.

functions.name: csgn
functions.summary: Returns the sign of a complex number: 1 or -1.
description: It is the sign of the real part, or of the imaginary part when the real part is 0; `csgn(0)` is 0. If the sign can't be decided, the call is returned unevaluated. In JavaScript it is `nerdamer.csgn`.

examples.description: Real part 0: the imaginary part decides.

functions.name: polarform
functions.summary: Writes a complex expression in polar form, r·e^(iθ).
description: A real number stays as it is.

examples.description: A real number stays as it is.

functions.name: rectform
functions.summary: Writes a complex expression in rectangular form, a + b·i.
description: It rewrites polar forms r·e^(iθ) with cosine and sine.

functions.name: abs
functions.summary: Returns the absolute value of an expression.
description: It drops the `abs` when the sign is known: from numbers, even powers, or [assumptions](/docs/functions/assume/). Otherwise it stays. For a complex number it is the modulus.

examples.description: An even power is never negative.
The modulus of a complex number.

functions.name: cbrt
functions.summary: Returns the cube root of an expression.
description: The result stays as `cbrt(...)`, so no approximation or choice of root is made. Call `evaluate` for a number: a negative real number gets its real cube root, and a complex number its principal cube root.

examples.description: Stays exact, with the real cube root kept.
The real cube root of a negative number; compare [`nthroot`](/docs/functions/nthroot/).

functions.name: ceil
functions.summary: Rounds a number up to the nearest integer.
description: For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated. `ceiling` is another name for it.

examples.description: Up is toward zero for a negative number.

functions.name: contains
functions.summary: Returns 1 if a vector, set, solution set or dictionary contains a value, and 0 otherwise.
description: For a dictionary it checks the keys. For anything else, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: numeric
functions.summary: Evaluates a number to a given number of significant digits.
description: It works on numbers, vectors, matrices and sets. Symbolic parts stay symbolic; only fully numeric values are evaluated. In JavaScript it is `nerdamer.numeric`.

examples.description: A symbolic value stays as it is.

functions.name: size
functions.summary: Returns the dimensions of a vector, matrix, set or dictionary.
description: The result is a vector: the length of a vector, or the rows and columns of a matrix.

functions.name: count
functions.summary: Returns the number of entries in a vector, set, solution set or dictionary.
description: For anything else, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: exp
functions.summary: Returns e raised to a power.
description: `exp(x)` is the same as `e^x`. Exact values are simplified, and numbers can be evaluated.

examples.description: Written as a power of e.

functions.name: expand
functions.summary: Multiplies out products and powers into a sum of terms.
description: It distributes products over sums and expands integer powers, all the way down. Functions such as `sin(2*x)` aren't rewritten, and nothing is evaluated numerically.

functions.name: floor
functions.summary: Rounds a number down to the nearest integer.
description: For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated.

examples.description: Down is away from zero for a negative number.

functions.name: log
functions.summary: Returns the natural logarithm, or the logarithm in a given base.
description: With one argument the base is e; a second argument sets the base. Exact values are simplified.
For a complex number it is the principal logarithm. Rules such as `log(x*y)=log(x)+log(y)` are used only when the signs allow them, for example with [assumptions](/docs/functions/assume/).

functions.name: matrix
functions.summary: Creates a matrix from its rows.
description: Each argument is one row, as a vector. All rows must have the same length.

functions.name: max
functions.summary: Returns the largest of its arguments.
description: Numbers, and symbols that [assumptions](/docs/functions/assume/) let it compare, are reduced. If it can't order all the arguments, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: min
functions.summary: Returns the smallest of its arguments.
description: Numbers, and symbols that [assumptions](/docs/functions/assume/) let it compare, are reduced. If it can't order all the arguments, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: nthroot
functions.summary: Returns the nth root, as the principal power `x^(1/n)`.
description: For a negative number and an odd `n`, that is the principal complex root, not the real one. Use [`cbrt`](/docs/functions/cbrt/) for the real cube root.

examples.description: The principal cube root of -8 is complex.

functions.name: parens
functions.summary: Keeps parentheses around an expression in the output.
description: It doesn't change the value, only how the result is written.

examples.description: Kept as the base of a power.

functions.name: round
functions.summary: Rounds a number, to an integer or to a number of decimal places.
description: Halves round away from zero. For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: sign
functions.summary: Returns 1, -1 or 0: the sign of a real expression.
description: For a symbol, [assumptions](/docs/functions/assume/) can decide it; otherwise the call is returned unevaluated. For a complex number, it is the [complex sign](/docs/functions/csgn/).

functions.name: sqrt
functions.summary: Returns the principal square root of an expression.
description: Perfect squares and square factors come out exactly: `sqrt(12)` is `2*3^(1/2)`. The square root of a negative number is imaginary.
For a symbol, the sign matters: `sqrt(x^2)` is `abs(x)` unless an [assumption](/docs/functions/assume/) settles the sign.

examples.description: With `x>=3`, no absolute value is needed.

functions.name: subst
functions.summary: Replaces a variable or a subexpression with another expression.
description: The replacement happens everywhere: in sums, products, powers and function arguments. You can replace a whole subexpression, not only a variable.

functions.name: trunc
functions.summary: Drops the fractional part of a number, rounding toward zero.
description: For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated.

examples.description: A negative number rounds toward zero.

functions.name: div
functions.summary: Divides one polynomial by another and returns the quotient and remainder.
description: The result is a vector `[quotient, remainder]`. Polynomials in several variables work too. If the inputs aren't polynomials, the result is `[0, dividend]`.

functions.name: divide
functions.summary: Divides one polynomial by another and returns the result as one expression.
description: It returns `quotient + remainder/divisor`. Unlike [`div`](/docs/functions/div/), it doesn't return the parts separately. If the inputs aren't polynomials, it divides normally.

functions.name: polyFactors
functions.summary: Returns the factors of a polynomial as separate entries of a vector.
description: In Notation it is `polyfactors`; in JavaScript, `polyFactors`. Compare [`factor`](/docs/functions/factor/), which returns their product.

examples.description: A difference of squares has two factors.

functions.name: forget
functions.summary: Removes the assumptions about a variable, or all assumptions.
description: `forget(x)` removes those about `x`. `forget(all)` removes every assumption. See [`assume`](/docs/functions/assume/).

functions.name: unassign
functions.summary: Removes the value assigned to a variable.
description: After `x:5`, `unassign(x)` makes `x` a plain variable again. It doesn't touch [assumptions](/docs/functions/assume/); use `forget` for those.

examples.description: Assign, remove, and `x` is a variable again.

functions.name: radians
functions.summary: Converts degrees to radians, exactly.
description: It multiplies by `pi/180` and keeps the result exact.

functions.name: degrees
functions.summary: Converts radians to degrees, exactly.
description: It multiplies by `180/pi` and keeps the result exact.

functions.name: log10
functions.summary: Returns the base-10 logarithm of an expression.
description: Exact powers of ten simplify. Otherwise the result is written as `log(x)/log(10)`.

examples.description: A symbol, written with natural logarithms.

functions.name: step
functions.summary: Returns the unit step: 0 for negative values and 1 for zero and positive ones.
description: Unlike [`heaviside`](/docs/functions/heaviside/), `step(0)` is 1, not 1/2, as in Nerdamer 1.x. For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: rect
functions.summary: Returns a rectangular pulse of width 1 centered at 0.
description: It is 1 inside the pulse (`|x|<1/2`), 1/2 at its edges and 0 outside. For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: tri
functions.summary: Returns a triangular pulse centered at 0.
description: It is `1-|x|` for `|x|<1`, and 0 elsewhere. For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: continued_fraction
functions.summary: Returns the continued fraction of a number.
description: The result is `(sign, whole part, [partial quotients])`. A second argument limits how many partial quotients are computed.

functions.name: scientific
functions.summary: Writes a number in scientific notation.
description: A second argument sets the significant digits, from 1 to 1e9 (10 by default). Only the display changes; the value stays exact for later calculations.

examples.description: Trailing zeros are kept to show the precision.

functions.name: solve
functions.summary: Solves an equation for one variable and returns every solution it finds.

parameters.name: equation
parameters.description: An equation such as `x^2=4`, or an expression, which is solved for zero.

parameters.name: variable
parameters.description: The variable to solve for.

parameters.name: onInterval
parameters.description: Optional. A window `[lower, upper]` for the numerical search; the default is `[-10, 10]`. Exact roots, such as polynomial roots, are returned wherever they are.

functions.returns: A SolutionSet, written `{...}`, holding each distinct solution. It is empty, `{}`, when there is none.

examples.description: An expression is solved for zero.
Other symbols stay symbolic, so this gives the quadratic formula.
A periodic equation returns the whole family of solutions. `_n` stands for any integer.
Store the SolutionSet, then pick one member by giving `_n` a value inside `evaluate`. `:` assigns; `=` makes an equation.
An unknown in an exponent is solved with logarithms.
`x=0` is left out, because the denominator vanishes there.
Roots that fail the original equation are dropped. Squaring both sides gives 3 and 8, and only 8 works.
Roots outside the domain of a logarithm are dropped too.
With no closed form, roots are found numerically: about 0.309906932380691, and the exact root 4.
`sin(x)=x/3` has three roots. With a window, only the one between 1 and 5 is searched for.
The window only limits the numerical search: polynomial roots are found exactly, so all three come back.
Solve the relativistic kinetic-energy equation for the velocity `v`.

notes: Numerical roots are approximate, to the working precision.
A comparison such as `x^2<4` is an error; `solve` takes equations, written with `=`.
The window must be two finite numbers in ascending order, such as `[1,5]`; anything else is an error.
`_n` is reserved: `_n:0` is an error. Give it a value inside `evaluate`, as above, where the value is local to that call and `= denotes an equation`, not an assignment.
In JavaScript, substitute an integer into a family member: `nerdamer.solve('sin(x)', 'x').elements[0].subst('_n', 2)` gives `2*pi`.
To solve several equations at once, use `solveeqs`.

javascriptExamples.description: The method takes the same arguments as strings.
Read the solutions one by one from `elements`.
Pick a member of a periodic family.
In JavaScript, pass the window as a parsed vector.

functions.name: factor
functions.summary: Factors a polynomial or an integer.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: A polynomial in one or more variables, or an integer.

functions.returns: The factored expression. A polynomial that can't be factored over the rationals comes back unchanged.

examples.description: The leading coefficient doesn't have to be 1.
Factors are split as far as rational coefficients allow.
`x^2-2` would need irrational coefficients, so it stays as it is.
A repeated factor is written as a power.
Common factors come out first, in several variables too.
A rational constant comes out in front.
An integer is split into primes.

notes: The order of the factors isn't fixed and can change between versions. To compare results, compare them with `expand`, not as text.
To get the prime factors of an integer as a list, use `pfactor`: `pfactor(12)` gives `[2, 2, 3]`.

functions.name: defint
functions.summary: Computes a definite integral between two numeric bounds.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: The integrand.

parameters.name: variable
parameters.description: The variable of integration.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: The lower bound, a number.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: The upper bound, a number.

functions.returns: The value of the integral: exact when possible, otherwise a decimal approximation. Input it can't integrate comes back unevaluated, as a `defint(...)` call.

examples.description: Bounds can be constants such as `e`.
`e^(-x^2)` has no elementary antiderivative, so the value is computed numerically.
`log(x)` is undefined at 0, but the integral converges.
A constant integrand can contain other symbols.
Other symbols mixed with the variable aren't handled yet; the call comes back unevaluated.
A symbolic bound also leaves the call unevaluated. Use `integrate` for the antiderivative.

notes: The order is expression, variable, from, to, and all four are required.
An integral that can't be computed comes back unevaluated rather than as an error, so check for a `defint(...)` result.
An integral that diverges, such as `defint(1/x,x,0,1)`, comes back unevaluated with a `defint.singularity` [warning](/docs/guides/warnings/).
The variable is local to the call: a value stored under its name, as in `x:5`, isn't substituted inside it.

functions.name: binom
functions.summary: Computes a binomial coefficient: the number of ways to choose `k` items from `n`.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: The number of items, a nonnegative integer.

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: How many to choose, an integer.

functions.returns: The exact coefficient, as an integer.

examples.description: With a symbolic argument, the call is kept as it is.

notes: A negative `n` is an error.

functions.name: nextprime
functions.summary: Returns the smallest prime greater than an integer.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: An integer. The result is always greater than it, even when `value` is prime.

functions.returns: The next prime, as an integer.

examples.description: 13 is prime, but the result is strictly greater.
A symbol or a non-integer keeps the call as it is.

notes: To split an integer into primes, use `factor` or `pfactor`.

functions.name: powmod
functions.summary: Computes `base^exponent mod modulus` exactly, without computing the full power.

parameters.name: base
parameters.description: An integer.

parameters.name: exponent
parameters.description: A nonnegative integer.

parameters.name: modulus
parameters.description: A positive integer.

functions.returns: The remainder, an integer from 0 up to `modulus - 1`.

examples.description: Large exponents are fast, because the full power is never built.
A negative base still gives a remainder from 0 up to `modulus - 1`.
A symbolic argument keeps the call as it is.

notes: A negative exponent or a modulus below 1 is an error.

functions.name: rank
functions.summary: Returns the rank of a matrix: the number of linearly independent rows.

parameters.name: matrix
parameters.description: A matrix of any shape.

examples.description: The second row is twice the first, so the rank is 1.
A matrix doesn't have to be square.
Symbolic entries are treated as generic: this assumes `a*d-b*c` is not zero.
A vector such as `[1,2]` is an error; wrap it in `matrix` to get a one-row matrix.

functions.name: taylor
functions.summary: Computes a Taylor polynomial of an expression around a point.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: The expression to expand.

parameters.name: variable
parameters.description: The variable to expand in.

parameters.name: center
parameters.description: The point to expand around. It can't depend on `variable`.

parameters.name: degree
parameters.description: The highest power to keep, a nonnegative integer.

functions.returns: The polynomial, exact. If the derivatives can't be computed, the call is kept as it is.

examples.description: Around another point, the terms are powers of `x-1`.
The center can be symbolic, such as `pi`.
A polynomial stops once its derivatives are zero, so a high `degree` is fine.
`log(x)` has no Taylor polynomial around 0, so the call is kept as it is.

notes: A negative or fractional `degree` is an error.
A symbolic or very large `degree` keeps the call as it is.
The variable is local to the call: a value stored under its name, as in `x:5`, isn't substituted inside it.

functions.name: trace
functions.summary: Returns the trace of a square matrix: the sum of its diagonal entries.

parameters.name: matrix
parameters.description: A square matrix.

functions.returns: The sum of the diagonal entries.

examples.description: The 3 by 3 identity matrix has trace 3.

notes: A matrix that isn't square is an error.

functions.name: vars
functions.summary: Lists the variables in an expression.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: Any expression.

functions.returns: A vector of the distinct variables, sorted by name. Constants such as `pi` are not included.

examples.description: Both sides of an equation count.
The result is sorted by name.
`pi` is a constant, not a variable.

notes: Use it to find which variables to pass to `solve`, `diff` or `buildFunction`.

javascriptExamples.description: In JavaScript, `.variables()` on an expression returns the names as strings.

functions.name: append
functions.summary: Returns a vector with one more element at the end.

parameters.name: vector
parameters.description: The vector to add to. It isn't changed.

parameters.name: element
parameters.description: The element to add. A vector is added as one element.

functions.returns: A new vector, one element longer.

examples.description: Add a number at the end.
A vector is added as one element, so this is a vector of two vectors.
The original vector stays as it was.
Build a list in a loop, starting from the empty vector `[]`.
If `v` has no value yet, the call is kept as it is.

notes: The first argument must be a vector: `append({1,2},3)` is an error. To add to a set, use [`union`](/docs/functions/union/).

functions.name: union
functions.summary: Returns the set of values that are in any of the given sets.

parameters.name: set1, set2, ...
parameters.description: Two or more sets, written `{...}`.

functions.returns: A set. Each value appears once.

examples.description: `2` is in both sets, and appears once.
Collect the distinct values from a loop, starting from the empty set `{}`.
If the sets have no value yet, the call is kept as it is.

notes: Every argument must be a set: `union({1},[1,2])` is an error.

functions.name: intersection
functions.summary: Returns the set of values that are in every one of the given sets.

parameters.name: set1, set2, ...
parameters.description: Two or more sets, written `{...}`.

functions.returns: A set, empty, `{}`, when no value is in all of them.

examples.description: Nothing in common gives the empty set.

notes: Every argument must be a set.

functions.name: difference
functions.summary: Returns the values of the first set that aren't in the second.

parameters.name: set1
parameters.description: The set to take values from.

parameters.name: set2
parameters.description: The values to leave out.

examples.description: Sets of symbols work the same way.
Leaving out everything gives the empty set.

notes: Both arguments must be sets. The order matters: `difference(A,B)` keeps what is in `A` only.

functions.name: intersects
functions.summary: Tests whether two sets have a value in common.

parameters.name: set1, set2
parameters.description: Two sets, written `{...}`.

functions.returns: `1` when the sets share a value, `0` when they don't.

examples.description: If the sets have no value yet, the call is kept as it is.

notes: Both arguments must be sets. The order doesn't matter.
It gives the same answer as checking that `intersection(A,B)` isn't empty.

functions.name: issubset
functions.summary: Tests whether every value of the first set is in the second.

parameters.name: set1
parameters.description: The set whose values are checked.

parameters.name: set2
parameters.description: The set to look for them in.

functions.returns: `1` when `set1` is a subset of `set2`, `0` otherwise.

examples.description: The order matters: `2` isn't in the second set.
The empty set is a subset of every set.
If the sets have no value yet, the call is kept as it is.

notes: Both arguments must be sets.
`issubset(A,B)` is the same as the comparison `A <= B`.

functions.name: simplify
functions.summary: Rewrites an expression in a simpler, equivalent form.
description: It cancels common factors, reduces fractions, applies identities such as `sin(x)^2+cos(x)^2=1`, cancels factorials, simplifies roots, and simplifies inside function arguments.
It only makes changes that are always valid, or valid under the [assumptions](/docs/functions/assume/) you have made.

functions.name: gcd
functions.summary: Returns the greatest common divisor of two polynomials or numbers.
description: It finds common numeric factors, monomials, and polynomial factors in one or more variables, including factors with symbolic coefficients.

examples.description: A common number and polynomial factor.
A common monomial in two variables.
A common factor with symbolic coefficients.
Expressions with no common polynomial factor give 1.

functions.name: lcm
functions.summary: Returns the least common multiple of two polynomials or numbers.
description: Shared factors appear once in the result. If either argument is zero, the result is zero.

functions.name: groebner
functions.summary: Computes a Gröbner basis of a polynomial system.
description: Pass the polynomials as a vector; the result is a vector too, in lexicographic order. A Gröbner basis rewrites a system into an equivalent, often triangular one that is easier to solve.
In JavaScript you can also pass the variable order.

examples.description: A circle and a line become a triangular system.

functions.name: partfrac
functions.summary: Splits a fraction of polynomials into partial fractions.
description: It handles distinct and repeated linear factors, irreducible quadratic factors, and fractions where the top has a higher degree than the bottom (it divides first).
If there is nothing to split, the expression comes back unchanged.

examples.description: Divides first; here there is no remainder.

functions.name: completeSquare
functions.summary: Rewrites a quadratic as a square plus a constant.
description: In Notation it is `sqcomp`. In JavaScript it is `completeSquare`, which also returns the parts of `a*(x+h)^2+k`; see [Results & output](/docs/public-helpers/).

functions.name: content
functions.summary: Returns the greatest common divisor of a polynomial's coefficients.
description: Only the numbers count: for `6*x^2+15*x-3` it is 3. If the input isn't a polynomial, the call is returned unevaluated.

examples.description: The coefficients share a factor of 3.

functions.name: deg
functions.summary: Returns the degree of a polynomial.
description: Without a variable, it is the total degree: the largest sum of powers in any term. With a variable, it is the highest power of that variable.
If the input isn't a polynomial, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: solveSystem
functions.summary: Solves a system of equations and returns the solutions.
description: It solves linear and nonlinear systems, exactly where it can and numerically otherwise. Systems with free variables, complex coefficients, more equations than unknowns, or trigonometric terms all work.
In Notation it is `solveeqs`; in JavaScript it is `solveSystem`, which can also take the list of unknowns, so other symbols are treated as parameters.
The result is a vector with one dictionary per solution, such as `[{x => 2, y => 1}]`. When a linear system has infinitely many solutions, the answer is written in terms of its free variables.

examples.description: Two equations, three unknowns: `z` stays free.
A parabola and a line meet at (-1,1) and (2,4).
A circle and a line: exact irrational solutions.
Three nonlinear equations with six isolated solutions.
A mixed trigonometric and polynomial system, solved numerically: x is about ±2.68259128682539 and y about -0.196296012151.
More equations than unknowns (overdetermined), but consistent.
A trigonometric equation in a system is solved numerically.

notes: When a nonlinear system has infinitely many solutions that aren't isolated, it throws an `UnsupportedOperationError`.
Numerical solving returns the roots it finds in its search. It doesn't turn `sin(x)=0` into a family of solutions; for one equation, use [`solve`](/docs/functions/solve/), which does.
A comparison such as `x+y<3` is an error; each item must be an equation or an expression.

functions.name: diff
functions.summary: Differentiates an expression with respect to a variable.
description: It uses the product, quotient, power and chain rules on algebraic expressions and the built-in functions. Pass an order for higher derivatives.

examples.description: The chain rule through a power of a sine.
A variable raised to a variable power.
Leave out the variable when the expression has only one.
A vector is differentiated element by element.
A value stored under the variable's name isn't substituted, so this is still `2*x`.
Other stored values are substituted as usual.

notes: Without a variable, `diff` uses the only variable left after stored values are substituted: after `x:5`, `diff(x^2)` gives `0`. With more than one variable, give it: `diff(x*y)` is an error.

functions.name: integrate
functions.summary: Finds an antiderivative of an expression.
description: It handles sums, constant factors, the elementary functions, scaled arguments, and many algebraic and trigonometric forms.
If it can't find an antiderivative, it returns the integral unevaluated rather than a wrong answer. For a value between two bounds, use [`defint`](/docs/functions/defint/).

examples.description: Leave out the variable when the expression has only one.

notes: Without a variable, the expression must have exactly one: `integrate(5)` and `integrate(x*y)` are errors.
The variable is local to the call: a value stored under its name, as in `x:5`, isn't substituted inside it.

functions.name: limit
functions.summary: Computes the limit of an expression as a variable approaches a value.
description: It handles removable singularities, `0/0` and `∞/∞` forms, and the growth of polynomials, logarithms and exponentials. For a one-sided limit, pass `left` or `right`.
If it can't find the limit, the call is returned unevaluated.

examples.description: Leading terms decide the limit at infinity.
The two sides differ, so there is no limit: unevaluated.

notes: The variable is local to the call: a value stored under its name, as in `x:5`, isn't substituted inside it.

functions.name: laplace
functions.summary: Computes the Laplace transform of an expression.
description: It transforms powers, exponentials, trigonometric and hyperbolic functions, sums of these, and their shifted and scaled forms. If it has no rule for the input, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: ilaplace
functions.summary: Computes the inverse Laplace transform of an expression.
description: It inverts fractions of polynomials, including repeated poles and shifted linear and quadratic factors, and the standard trigonometric and hyperbolic pairs. If it can't, the call is returned unevaluated.

examples.description: An irreducible quadratic gives a damped sine.

functions.name: sum
functions.summary: Adds up an expression over a range of an integer index.
description: With number bounds, it adds the terms. With a symbolic bound, it finds a closed form where it can, as for powers of the index; otherwise the call is returned unevaluated.

examples.description: A closed form for a symbolic bound.
The index is local to the call, so a stored `k` doesn't change the terms.
Stored values still apply in the bounds.

functions.name: product
functions.summary: Multiplies an expression over a range of an integer index.
description: With number bounds, it multiplies the terms. With a symbolic bound, it finds a closed form where it can; otherwise the call is returned unevaluated.

examples.description: Multiply the entries of a vector.
A symbolic bound gives a factorial.

notes: The index is local to the call: a value stored under its name, as in `k:5`, isn't substituted. Stored values still apply in the bounds.

functions.name: assume
functions.summary: Tells Nerdamer that a variable lies in a range of real numbers.
description: Other operations use the range: comparisons, `max` and `min`, square roots and logarithm rules that depend on sign.
Repeated assumptions about one variable combine. An assumption that contradicts the current ones is an error, and the earlier ones stay.

Bounds stay exact: fractions and roots such as `sqrt(2)` aren't rounded. You can also relate two variables by a constant, as in `assume(x<y+1)` or `assume(2*x+3<2*y+5)`, and the bound carries over from one variable to the other.

Nerdamer only concludes what the ranges prove. It can prove the sign of sums of assumed variables, products of positive values, some integer and reciprocal powers, and square roots of nonnegative values. A result can be true, false or unknown; comparisons give 1 only for true.

examples.description: `x` is positive and `y` negative, so `x` is larger.
With `x>=3`, the root needs no absolute value.
Both positive, so the logarithms combine.
A bound passed on through another variable.
Two ranges prove the sign of a sum.
A bound on a square root.

notes: Assumptions last until you remove them. `forget(x)` removes those about `x`, and with them any relation `x` is part of; `forget(all)` removes all of them. In JavaScript, use `forgetAssumptionFor(x)` and `clearAssumptions()`.
Reciprocal bounds need a range that excludes zero, and square-root bounds need a range of nonnegative values.
An even power such as `x^2` is never negative, but that doesn't make it positive: it can be zero.
Relations other than a constant difference, such as `assume(x<y^2)`, are errors.
`getAssumptionFor(x)` returns only the range you stated for `x`, not one derived from relations.
From JavaScript, `nerdamer.assume` takes a variable, a comparison and a number. Notation also accepts expressions such as `1/3` or `sqrt(2)` as the bound.

functions.name: transpose
functions.summary: Swaps the rows and columns of a matrix.
description: In JavaScript, a matrix also has a `.transpose()` method.

functions.name: augment
functions.summary: Joins two matrices side by side.
description: Both must have the same number of rows.

functions.name: rref
functions.summary: Returns the reduced row-echelon form of a matrix.
description: Pass a prime number as a second argument to work modulo that prime.

examples.description: An invertible matrix reduces to the identity.

functions.name: nullspace
functions.summary: Returns a basis of the nullspace of a matrix.
description: The result is a vector of basis vectors. Pass a prime number as a second argument to work modulo that prime.

examples.description: A rank-1 matrix has a two-dimensional nullspace.

functions.name: determinant
functions.summary: Computes the determinant of a square matrix.
description: Entries can be symbolic. A matrix that isn't square is an error. The matrix you pass isn't changed.

functions.name: imatrix
functions.summary: Creates an identity matrix of a given size.
description: With a symbolic size, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: dot
functions.summary: Computes the dot product of two vectors.
description: The vectors must have the same length. With symbols that aren't vectors, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: cross
functions.summary: Computes the cross product of two three-dimensional vectors.
description: Both vectors must have three entries. The result is perpendicular to both.

examples.description: The first two unit vectors give the third.

functions.name: pfactor
functions.summary: Returns the prime factors of a positive integer, smallest first, with repeats.
description: To get each prime with its count instead, use [`pfactord`](/docs/functions/pfactord/). For polynomials, use [`factor`](/docs/functions/factor/).

functions.name: pfactord
functions.summary: Returns the prime factors of a positive integer with their counts.
description: The result is a dictionary from each prime to how often it occurs.

functions.name: roots
functions.summary: Returns the roots of a polynomial as a vector.
description: It works like Nerdamer 1.x's `roots`. For new code, [`solve`](/docs/functions/solve/) returns a solution set and handles more than polynomials.
For a number, it returns its two square roots.
Numerical roots use Aberth's method. Pass `jenkinstraub` as the third argument to use the Jenkins-Traub method instead.

examples.description: The square roots of a number.
With the Jenkins-Traub method instead of the default, Aberth's method.

notes: `jenkinstraub` needs real coefficients: `roots(x^2+i,x,jenkinstraub)` is an error. Leave the method out to use Aberth's method, which handles complex coefficients.
Only `roots` takes a method; `solve` doesn't.
A comparison such as `x^2<4` is an error.

functions.name: coeffs
functions.summary: Returns the coefficients of a polynomial, from the constant term up.
description: Missing powers give 0.

examples.description: Symbolic coefficients; the missing `x` term gives 0.

functions.name: invert
functions.summary: Returns the inverse of a square matrix.
description: The matrix you pass isn't changed.

functions.name: line
functions.summary: Returns the line through two points, as an expression in `x`.
description: Pass the points as two-element vectors. A third argument names the variable instead of `x`.

functions.name: mean
functions.summary: Returns the average of the values.
description: Pass the values separately or as one vector. Fractions stay exact, and symbols work.

functions.name: median
functions.summary: Returns the middle value.
description: Pass the values separately or as one vector. With an even number of values, it is the average of the two middle ones. If the values can't be put in order, the call is returned unevaluated.

examples.description: An even count: the average of 2 and 3.

functions.name: mode
functions.summary: Returns the value that occurs most often.
description: Pass the values separately or as one vector. When several values tie, the result is `mode(...)` of the tied values.

functions.name: variance
functions.summary: Returns the population variance: the average squared distance from the mean.
description: Pass the values separately or as one vector. It divides by n; for the sample variance, which divides by n-1, use [`smpvar`](/docs/functions/smpvar/).

functions.name: smpvar
functions.summary: Returns the sample variance, which divides by n-1.
description: Pass the values separately or as one vector. In JavaScript it is `sampleVariance`, from `nerdamer/statistics`. For the population variance, use [`variance`](/docs/functions/variance/).

functions.name: stdev
functions.summary: Returns the population standard deviation: the square root of the [variance](/docs/functions/variance/).
description: Pass the values separately or as one vector. The result stays exact.

functions.name: smpstdev
functions.summary: Returns the sample standard deviation: the square root of the [sample variance](/docs/functions/smpvar/).
description: Pass the values separately or as one vector. In JavaScript it is `sampleStandardDeviation`, from `nerdamer/statistics`.

examples.description: Compare with `stdev` of the same data, which is 2.

functions.name: zscore
functions.summary: Returns how many standard deviations a value is from the mean: (x - mean)/sd.
description: You pass the mean and standard deviation; it doesn't compute them from data.

examples.description: One standard deviation above the mean.

functions.name: significant
functions.summary: Rounds a number to a number of significant figures.
description: Unlike [`round`](/docs/functions/round/), which counts decimal places, it counts digits from the first nonzero one.

functions.name: realsolutions
functions.summary: Returns the real solutions in an interval.
description: For the result of [`solve`](/docs/functions/solve/), use `realsolutions(solutions, lower, upper)`. It also lists the members of a periodic family that fall in the interval.
For the result of [`solveeqs`](/docs/functions/solveeqs/), use `realsolutions(solutions, variable, lower, upper)`. It returns the real values of that one variable.

examples.description: List a periodic family between -2π and 2π.
The zeros of cosine in one period.
The x-values of a system's solutions.

notes: The interval must be finite.
In JavaScript, `SolutionSet.generate({ interval: [lower, upper] })` and `SolutionSet.generate({ indices: [first, last] })` do the same.

functions.name: and
functions.summary: Returns 1 when every argument is true, and 0 otherwise.
description: Arguments are checked left to right, and checking stops at the first false one, so later arguments aren't evaluated.

examples.description: Stops at the first false argument, so `1/0` never runs.

parameters.name: a, b, ...
parameters.description: Two or more conditions or values.

notes: A value is true when it isn't zero. An unknown symbol counts as true; a comparison that can't be decided, such as `x>0` for an unknown `x`, counts as false.

functions.name: or
functions.summary: Returns 1 when at least one argument is true, and 0 otherwise.
description: Arguments are checked left to right, and checking stops at the first true one.

parameters.name: a, b, ...
parameters.description: Two or more conditions or values.

notes: A value is true when it isn't zero. An unknown symbol counts as true; a comparison that can't be decided, such as `x>0` for an unknown `x`, counts as false.

functions.name: not
functions.summary: Returns 1 for a false value and 0 for a true one.

examples.description: `x>0` can't be decided for an unknown `x`, so it counts as false.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: A condition or value.

notes: A value is true when it isn't zero. An unknown symbol counts as true; a comparison that can't be decided, such as `x>0` for an unknown `x`, counts as false.

functions.name: xor
functions.summary: Returns 1 when an odd number of arguments are true.
description: Every argument is evaluated.

parameters.name: a, b, ...
parameters.description: Two or more conditions or values.

notes: A value is true when it isn't zero. An unknown symbol counts as true; a comparison that can't be decided, such as `x>0` for an unknown `x`, counts as false.

functions.name: if
functions.summary: Returns one of two values, depending on a condition.
description: Only the chosen branch is evaluated, so an error or assignment in the other one never happens.
The false branch is optional. Without it, a false condition gives no value, so use that form for a step that only sometimes runs, inside `block`.

examples.description: `x>0` can't be decided for an unknown `x`, so it counts as false.
No false branch: the assignment is skipped.

notes: A value is true when it isn't zero. An unknown symbol counts as true; a comparison that can't be decided, such as `x>0` for an unknown `x`, counts as false.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Decides which branch runs.

parameters.name: whenTrue
parameters.description: The value when the condition is true.

parameters.name: whenFalse
parameters.description: Optional. The value when it is false.

functions.name: iferror
functions.summary: Returns a fallback value when an expression throws an error.
description: If `expression` works, its value is returned and `fallback` isn't evaluated.

examples.description: The expression works, so the fallback never runs.
`0/0` throws, so the fallback is used.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: The expression to try.

parameters.name: fallback
parameters.description: The value to use if it throws an error.

notes: `return`, `break` and `continue` pass through `iferror`: they aren't treated as errors.

functions.name: iserror
functions.summary: Returns 1 when an expression throws an error, and 0 otherwise.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: The expression to test.

notes: `return`, `break` and `continue` aren't counted as errors.

functions.name: block
functions.summary: Evaluates expressions in order and returns the last value.
description: Use it to run several steps inside one expression, such as a function body or a loop body.

examples.description: Assign two values, then use them.

parameters.name: first, second, ...
parameters.description: Expressions evaluated in order.

parameters.name: last
parameters.description: The expression whose value is returned.

functions.name: while
functions.summary: Repeats an expression while a condition is true.
description: The condition is checked before each pass. `while` returns the value of the last pass.

examples.description: The same loop with a comparison.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Checked before each pass; the loop stops when it is false.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description: The expression to repeat. Use `block` for several steps.

notes: `break()` leaves the loop and `continue()` skips to the next pass.
If the body never runs, `while` has no value, and using it as one is an error.
A loop stops with an error after `MAX_LOOP_ITERATIONS` passes (1,000,000 by default); see [Settings](/docs/settings/).

functions.name: for
functions.summary: Repeats an expression with a start, a condition and a step.
description: `start` runs once. Then, while `condition` is true, `body` runs, followed by `step`.

examples.description: The loop variable is still set afterwards.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Runs once before the loop, usually an assignment such as `k:0`.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Checked before each pass; the loop stops when it is false.

parameters.name: step
parameters.description: Runs after each pass, such as `k:k+1`.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description: The expression to repeat.

notes: `continue()` still runs `step`; `break()` and `return` skip it.
The same `MAX_LOOP_ITERATIONS` limit as `while` applies.

functions.name: each
functions.summary: Evaluates an expression once for each element of a vector, matrix, set or dictionary.
description: Each element is given the name you choose while the body runs. A matrix is visited row by row.

examples.description: Add up a matrix, row by row.
`break()` works here too: stop at the first element above 2.

parameters.name: container
parameters.description: A vector, matrix, set or dictionary.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The name each element has inside the body.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description: The expression to evaluate for each element.

notes: The element name exists only inside the body.

functions.name: evaluate
functions.summary: Evaluates a value now, optionally with values for its variables.
description: With one argument, it evaluates numerically. With a dictionary such as `{x=>2}`, it uses those values for this call only. With a list of variables and a list of values, it does the same faster when you evaluate many points.

examples.description: Values for this call, on a vector.
Pick one solution from a periodic family by giving `_n` a value.
Variables and values as two lists.

notes: The values apply to this call only. They don't assign the variables, so `{_n=>0}` works even though `_n:0` is an error.
If it can't evaluate further, `evaluate` returns its input unchanged.
To store a value first, assign it with `:`; `=` makes an equation.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: An expression, equation, vector, matrix, set or solution set.

parameters.name: substitutions
parameters.description: Optional. A dictionary of values, such as `{x=>2}`.

parameters.name: variables
parameters.description: In the three-argument form: a vector of variables.

parameters.name: point
parameters.description: In the three-argument form: a vector of their values, in the same order.

functions.name: break
functions.summary: Leaves the loop it is in.
description: Works in `while`, `for` and `each`. It leaves only the innermost loop, and can't leave a function you defined.

examples.description: Leave the loop after the first pass.

functions.name: continue
functions.summary: Skips the rest of the current pass of a loop.
description: Works in `while`, `for` and `each`. In a `for` loop, the step still runs.

functions.name: return
functions.summary: Ends a function or block early with a value.
description: In a function you defined, `return` ends the function. Outside one, it ends the outermost `block`.

examples.description: Return early for a negative input.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to return.

functions.name: let
functions.summary: Gives variables temporary values for one expression.
description: The values exist only inside `body`. Afterwards, the variables have their old values again, so `let` is safe for loop counters and temporary results.

parameters.name: name, value, ...
parameters.description: One or more variable names, each followed by its value.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description: The expression that uses them.

functions.name: Chi
functions.summary: Returns the hyperbolic cosine integral.
description: It is even, and tends to minus infinity at 0. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: Ci
functions.summary: Returns the cosine integral.
description: It tends to minus infinity at 0 and to 0 at the infinities. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: Ei
functions.summary: Returns the exponential integral.
description: It tends to minus infinity at 0, to 0 at minus infinity, and to infinity at infinity. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: Li
functions.summary: Returns the logarithmic integral.
description: It tends to minus infinity at 1. A negative argument stays as it is. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

examples.description: A negative argument stays as it is.

functions.name: Shi
functions.summary: Returns the hyperbolic sine integral.
description: It is odd: `Shi(-x)` is `-Shi(x)`. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: Si
functions.summary: Returns the sine integral, the integral of sin(t)/t from 0 to x.
description: It is odd, and tends to π/2 and -π/2 at the infinities. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: delta
functions.summary: Returns the Dirac delta.
description: It is 0 away from zero. At zero it stays as `delta(0)`, because the delta has no finite value there. For a symbol, it is 0 when an [assumption](/docs/functions/assume/) shows the symbol isn't zero.

examples.description: Stays as it is at zero.

functions.name: dfact
functions.summary: Returns the double factorial, n·(n-2)·(n-4)·….
description: Integers are computed exactly. Other numbers use the gamma function: call `evaluate` for their value. The largest exact input is set by `MAX_DFACT_INPUT` (see [Settings](/docs/settings/)).

functions.name: erf
functions.summary: Returns the error function.
description: It tends to 1 and -1 at the infinities. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: erfc
functions.summary: Returns the complementary error function, 1-erf(x).

examples.description: Far into the tail, the value is tiny but not zero.

functions.name: factorial
functions.summary: Returns the factorial, n!.
description: Integers are computed exactly, and half-integers give exact values with `sqrt(pi)`. Other numbers use the gamma function. You can also write `n!` or `fact(n)`; the result is written with `fact`.
The largest exact input is set by `MAX_FACTORIAL_INPUT` (see [Settings](/docs/settings/)).

examples.description: A half-integer gives an exact value.
Other numbers use the gamma function.

functions.name: fib
functions.summary: Returns a Fibonacci number.
description: Integer indexes are computed exactly, including negative ones. For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated. The largest index is set by `MAX_FIB_INPUT` (see [Settings](/docs/settings/)).

functions.name: gamma
functions.summary: Returns the gamma function.
description: For a positive integer n, `gamma(n)` is `(n-1)!`. Half-integers give exact values with `sqrt(pi)`. Zero and negative integers, where gamma is undefined, throw an error. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: heaviside
functions.summary: Returns the Heaviside step: 0 for negative values, 1/2 at zero, and 1 for positive values.
description: For a symbol, [assumptions](/docs/functions/assume/) can decide it. Compare [`step`](/docs/functions/step/), which is 1 at zero.

functions.name: hypot
functions.summary: Returns the length of the vector (x, y): sqrt(x^2+y^2).

functions.name: mod
functions.summary: Returns the remainder of a division.
description: The result has the sign of the divisor, so `mod(-7,3)` is 2. Decimals work. For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated. A zero divisor is an error.

examples.description: The result takes the divisor's sign.

functions.name: modinv
functions.summary: Returns the inverse of a modulo m: the x for which a·x leaves remainder 1.
description: The inverse exists only when a and m have no common factor; otherwise it is an error.

functions.name: sinc
functions.summary: Returns sin(x)/x.
description: This is the unnormalized sinc. It is even, and `sinc(0)` is 1. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: isPrime
functions.summary: Returns 1 if an integer is prime, and 0 otherwise.
description: In Notation it is `isprime`; in JavaScript, `isPrime`. For a symbol, the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: gamma_incomplete
functions.summary: Returns the upper incomplete gamma function Γ(a, z).
description: For a positive integer a, it is written out exactly. Otherwise the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: gamma_incomplete_lower
functions.summary: Returns the lower incomplete gamma function γ(a, z).
description: For a positive integer a, it is written out exactly, as Γ(a) - Γ(a, z). Otherwise the call is returned unevaluated.

functions.name: cos
functions.summary: Returns the cosine of an angle in radians.
description: Exact values come out at multiples of π/6, π/4 and π/3; other angles stay as they are until you evaluate them.
`cos(-x)` simplifies to `cos(x)`, and `cos(acos(x))` to `x`.

examples.description: Not a special angle: stays exact.

functions.name: sin
functions.summary: Returns the sine of an angle in radians.
description: Exact values come out at multiples of π/6, π/4 and π/3; other angles stay as they are until you evaluate them.
`sin(-x)` simplifies to `-sin(x)`.

examples.description: Not a special angle: stays exact.

functions.name: tan
functions.summary: Returns the tangent of an angle in radians.
description: Exact values come out at multiples of π/6, π/4 and π/3; other angles stay as they are until you evaluate them.
At odd multiples of π/2, where tangent is undefined, it throws an error.

functions.name: sec
functions.summary: Returns the secant, 1/cos(x).
description: Where cosine is zero, at odd multiples of π/2, it throws an error.

functions.name: csc
functions.summary: Returns the cosecant, 1/sin(x).
description: Where sine is zero, at multiples of π, it throws an error.

functions.name: cot
functions.summary: Returns the cotangent, cos(x)/sin(x).
description: At multiples of π, where sine is zero, it throws an error.

functions.name: acos
functions.summary: Returns the arccosine, in radians from 0 to π.
description: For a number outside [-1, 1], the result stays exact; evaluating it gives a complex value.

functions.name: asin
functions.summary: Returns the arcsine, in radians from -π/2 to π/2.
description: For a number outside [-1, 1], the result stays exact; evaluating it gives a complex value.

functions.name: atan
functions.summary: Returns the arctangent, in radians between -π/2 and π/2.
description: Exact values come out as multiples of π, and `atan(Infinity)` is π/2.

examples.description: An exact value from an irrational input.

functions.name: asec
functions.summary: Returns the inverse secant, acos(1/x).

functions.name: acsc
functions.summary: Returns the inverse cosecant, asin(1/x).

functions.name: acot
functions.summary: Returns the inverse cotangent, in radians from 0 to π.
description: Zero and the infinities have exact values.

examples.description: A negative input gives an angle above π/2.

functions.name: atan2
functions.summary: Returns the angle of the point (x, y), in radians from -π to π.
description: Unlike `atan(y/x)`, it uses the signs of both coordinates, so it knows which quadrant the point is in. Note the order: `atan2(y, x)`.

examples.description: Third quadrant, which atan(y/x) can't tell from the first.

functions.name: cosh
functions.summary: Returns the hyperbolic cosine.
description: Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

examples.description: With an imaginary argument it is a cosine.

functions.name: sinh
functions.summary: Returns the hyperbolic sine.
description: Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: tanh
functions.summary: Returns the hyperbolic tangent.
description: It tends to 1 and -1 at the infinities. Call `evaluate` for a decimal value.

functions.name: sech
functions.summary: Returns the hyperbolic secant, 1/cosh(x).
description: It is 1 at zero and tends to 0 at the infinities.

functions.name: csch
functions.summary: Returns the hyperbolic cosecant, 1/sinh(x).
description: It tends to 0 at the infinities. At zero, where it is undefined, it throws an error.

functions.name: coth
functions.summary: Returns the hyperbolic cotangent, 1/tanh(x).
description: It tends to 1 and -1 at the infinities. At zero, where it is undefined, it throws an error.

functions.name: acosh
functions.summary: Returns the inverse hyperbolic cosine.
description: Below 1 the result is complex.

functions.name: asinh
functions.summary: Returns the inverse hyperbolic sine.
description: It tends to the infinities at the infinities.

functions.name: atanh
functions.summary: Returns the inverse hyperbolic tangent.

functions.name: asech
functions.summary: Returns the inverse hyperbolic secant, acosh(1/x).
description: The result stays exact, even at simple values; call `evaluate` for a number.

examples.description: Stays exact, even though its value is 0.

functions.name: acsch
functions.summary: Returns the inverse hyperbolic cosecant, asinh(1/x).
description: The result stays exact; call `evaluate` for a number.

functions.name: acoth
functions.summary: Returns the inverse hyperbolic cotangent, atanh(1/x).
description: It tends to 0 at the infinities.
